The Edible dormouse (Glis glis) is a medium-sized glirid rodent notable for its prolonged hibernation and slow life-history strategy. Newborn pups emerge from the birth canal at a remarkably modest size, typically weighing only about 1.5 grams [Wwb = about 1.5 grams] immediately following parturition, a mass that reflects the altricial state of the neonate. These tiny offspring, blind and nearly hairless at delivery, are entirely dependent on milk from the lactating female during their first weeks of life. The gestation period, timed from the completion of internal fertilisation to the birthing event, lasts approximately 25 days [tg = approximately 25 days] under the typical body temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C] maintained during the active season. This relatively short intrauterine development is consistent with the pattern observed in other small hibernating mammals, where energetic constraints imposed by a seasonal lifestyle favour a rapid embryogenesis. The suckling juvenile then enters a prolonged phase of dependency, during which it relies exclusively on its mother's nutritional output before making the dietary transition to solid foods.

Weaning, defined as the cessation of maternal milk provisioning and the onset of full nutritional independence, represents a critical developmental milestone for the suckling juvenile. In Glis glis, this weaning process concludes at approximately 33 days after birth [tx = approximately 33 days after birth], at which point the young begin foraging on their own for berries, nuts, and oth at a temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C]er forest mast. This age at weaning is measured when the juveniles are maintained at the species' characteristic active-phase body temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C], a thermal regime that supports the metabolic demands of growth and digestive maturation. The dietary transition from milk to solid food is gradual, with the mother continuing to provide some food items even as the offspring increasingly feed independently. By the end of this period, the weaned juvenile has achieved a body mass substantially greater than its 1.5 gram [Wwb = 1.5 gram] birth weight, though it remains far from the dimensions of a fully grown adult.

The attainment of sexual maturity in the Edible dormouse is a remarkably protracted process compared to many other rodents of equivalent body size. In females, puberty is achieved at approximately 335 days after birth [tp = 335 days after birth], whereas males reach this stage slightly earlier, at roughly 322 days after birth [tp = roughly 322 days after birth], under a stable internal temperature of 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C]. This delay in reproductive maturation is strongly linked to the species' hibernatory lifestyle, as the long winter torpor period drastically compresses the annual window available for somatic growth and gonadal activation. The onset of gametogenesis in both sexes does not occur until after the second hibernation season, meaning that juveniles born in late summer typically do not become reproductively active until their third calendar year. This slow pace of maturation contrasts sharply with many other glirids and underscores the selective pressures imposed by a highly seasonal, mast-driven environment.

Adult body size in Glis glis is one of its most distinguishing morphological traits. The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown, reproductively active adult is approximately 125 grams [Wwi = approximately 125 grams], though considerable seasonal variation exists, with individuals doubling their mass in autumn through intensive hyperphagia to build fat reserves for hibernation. This maximum recorded body mass in adults represents a peak that is typically reached during the late summer fattening period, just before the animals enter their winter torpor. The breeding adult mammal that emerges in spring at a much lower mass must then rapidly regain condition to support gestation and lactation. The reproductive output of females is constrained by this body size and by the energetic demands of nursing a litter. Field studies reveal that females produce roughly 1.2 litters per year [F_R_i = roughly 1.2 litters per year], with a typical litter size of 4 to 5 pups [N_R_i = litter size of 4 to 5 pups]. This low annual fecundity is a direct consequence of the short active season and the high cost of lactation in a temperate forest environment.

Lifespan data for the Edible dormouse indicate a maximum recorded longevity that is exceptional for a rodent of its mass. The oldest documented individuals in wild populations have been recorded at approximately 3,176 days [am = approximately 3,176 days], though captive specimens maintained under controlled thermal conditions at 37.7 °C [T = 37.7 °C] may approach or slightly exceed this figure. This extended lifespan considerably surpasses that of other similarly sized rodents, a pattern consistent with the species' slow life-history strategy characterised by delayed maturation and low annual fecundity. The maximum reproductive rate, derived from roughly 1.2 litters per year [F_R_i = roughly 1.2 litters per year] and a mean litter size of 4 to 5 pups [N_R_i = litter size of 4 to 5 pups], yields a modest annual output. Such a conservative reproductive strategy likely evolved as an adaptation to the unpredictable and mast-driven food supply of European beech and oak forests, where bumper crops occur irregularly and favour a bet-hedging approach over high fecundity.
